evals.name: Full run
evals.prompt: We run a savings program at three garment factories in Gazipur, Bangladesh, about 6,000 workers, mostly young women, paid monthly into a mobile-money wallet the factories brought in 18 months ago. We want to enroll workers by default in a savings pocket in the wallet, with opt-out at the HR desk, and judge it by the balance held after six months. Our proposal says to expect the 40-point effect from Blumenstock, Callen and Ghani (2018), https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20171676. Does that apply to us? This is for a one-factory pilot.
evals.expected_output: A transferability assessment in the output template with one of the five verdicts.
assertions: Opens with a few plain sentences to the user before the assessment, and states how the study was read: full text, abstract only, or the user's summary.
Gives the study's effect with its unit (40 percentage points on participation).
Has a table comparing the study and the Bangladesh setting, with each row marked holds, does not hold, or unknown.
Notes that the study measured participation and the team's outcome is the balance held after six months.
Gives exactly one of the five verdicts, and lists at least two assumptions to test locally, each with a check.
Ends with two or three next moves, each with its reason, and questions the user could ask next, with no single instruction.

evals.name: Missing context
evals.prompt: Does the savings default effect work in Bangladesh?
evals.expected_output: The skill asks for the study and the setting, and produces nothing else.
assertions: Asks which study or finding the user means.
Asks about the setting: who, what would be delivered, by whom, or which outcome.
Gives no verdict.
Does not cite a study the user did not name.
Says why it needs these answers.

evals.name: Near the escalation point
evals.prompt:
We're a Lagos NGO about to ask a funder for $2 million to scale SMS appointment reminders to 400 clinics. Our case rests on one South African trial where reminders plus a follow-up phone call from a nurse cut missed HIV clinic visits. We'd send SMS only, through an aggregator, and we have no nurses for calls. I've pasted the trial's abstract below; we can't get the full paper. Will it hold?

[abstract pasted]
evals.expected_output: The skill assesses what it can from the abstract, says what the abstract leaves unknown, and tells the user to bring in a specialist before a scale-up decision.
assertions: States that the study was read from the abstract only.
Notes that the user's treatment drops the nurse's phone call.
Does not give 'Likely to hold' as the verdict.
Tells the user to consult a researcher who knows the setting, or an evaluator, before the scale-up decision.
Says what to bring to that specialist.

evals.name: Wrong skill
evals.prompt: We're planning a pilot of default savings enrollment for mobile-money users in Tanzania. What effect size should we plan the sample size on?
evals.expected_output: The skill says this is a planning number, not a fit judgment on one study, and points to the skill for that.
assertions: Says the request is for a planning number.
Names estimate-expected-effect.
Does not produce a transferability assessment.

evals.name: From an expert review #14
evals.prompt: We work on anti-corruption in district land offices in Uganda. Will reducing petty corruption raise people's trust in government here? Our setting: rural districts, land offices staffed by district officials, and we'd measure trust with a household survey. I don't have a particular study, it's just what everyone says.
evals.expected_output: The skill says there is no finding to assess and gives no verdict.
assertions: Says no study was supplied, or that no study tests the claim.
Writes 'No evidence to assess' or asks for the study; gives none of the other four verdicts.
Does not state that the effect is unlikely to transfer.
Any related study it lists is described by how it differs from the claim.
Points to assess-evidence-base for finding what evidence exists.
